description: We are Team of two with enough interest in space so that we can build anything
summary:
ARES is an interactive digital map of Mars, designed like a Google Earth for the Red Planet. It allows anyone—from students and space fans to scientists and mission planners—to explore Mars from the comfort of their screen using real photos, satellite scans, and measurements collected by NASA and international space missions.

With ARES, you can spin the entire planet in realistic 3D, zoom in to see massive landmarks like the giant volcano of Olympus Mons or the colossal canyon of Valles Marineris, and even drop down to ground level to see what the rocky red landscape looks like from a rover’s perspective.

Beyond sightseeing, the platform serves as an interactive exploration tool. You can follow the real tracks of famous Mars rovers like Curiosity and Perseverance, stepping through their missions day by day to see where they stopped and studied rocks. The system also maps out key scientific discoveries across the planet, including underground water ice, mineral deposits, seismic marsquake locations, and potential landing zones for future astronauts.

Planning trips across Mars is tricky because of steep crater walls and boulder fields. ARES helps solve this by calculating safe driving paths between any two points. It automatically checks the slopes and roughness of the terrain, showing direct routes versus safer, flatter paths that keep vehicles from rolling over. Overall, ARES brings the wonder of Mars to life, making real space science accessible and exciting for everyone.
details:
1. What does it do, or how does it work?

ARES (Advanced Reconnaissance and Exploration System) is an interactive, scientific-grade Mars exploration and terrain-intelligence platform. It functions as a specialised, non-terrestrial GIS environment that unifies planetary topography, multispectral satellite data, seismic activity, and rover traverses into a synchronised, map-first workspace.

The system operates across three interconnected viewing modes:

  • Global 3D SceneView: A rotatable Martian globe built on the real HRSC–MOLA 200-metre elevation mesh, complete with vertical exaggeration and choreographed fly-tos to iconic planetary wonders.
  • Regional 2D MapView: A planar cartographic interface for precision regional inspection and coordinate tracking.
  • Local Analysis Ground POV: A first-person rover camera deck that drops the observer directly onto the surface with 360° orbital panning, elevation pitch controls, and accurate horizon rendering.

ARES ingests 14 scientific datasets from NASA and ESA, classifying every layer under strict provenance guidelines (Observed, Derived, Modelled, or Simulated). Users can inspect high-resolution CTX/HiRISE imagery footprints, CRISM mineral spectroscopy (clays, carbonates, sulphates), SWIM subsurface ice deposits, and InSight seismic events. Additionally, ARES features an autonomous Terrain-Aware A* Route Planner that computes continuous slope gradients using Horn’s algorithm to generate three candidate traversal paths (Safest, Balanced, and Direct) calibrated against rover rollover safety limits.

2. What benefits does it have?

  • Planetary Coordinate Integrity: Unlike conventional mapping tools that warp extraterrestrial bodies onto Earth ellipsoids (causing up to 47% distortion), ARES strictly enforces the IAU Mars 2000 datum (WKID 104905 / 104971). All distances, areas, and elevation transects represent true Martian geodesy.
  • Unified Planetary Context: Combines terrain elevation, mineralogy, ice deposits, and seismic hazard data into a single interactive viewport, eliminating the need to cross-reference disconnected scientific databases.
  • Autonomous Navigation & Risk Mitigation: Enables researchers and mission designers to simulate traverse viability, calculate slope penalties, and avoid rover tipping hazards prior to mission execution.
  • Mission Chronology & Fleet Tracking: Provides interactive sol-by-sol timeline scrubbers and waypoint telemetry for six surface missions (Perseverance, Curiosity, InSight, Spirit, Opportunity, and Zhurong).
  • Zero-Barrier Web Accessibility: Runs natively in modern web browsers without requiring specialised, heavy GIS software suites or proprietary plugins.

3. What is the intended impact of the project?

  • Accelerating Mission Planning: Empowers aerospace engineers and planetary scientists to rapidly screen potential landing zones, evaluate slope safety, and plan surface traverse paths for future Mars sample return and crewed exploration missions.
  • Site Selection for In-Situ Resource Utilisation (ISRU): Identifies optimal locations for potential human habitats by co-locating accessible subsurface water ice (SWIM), stable terrain slopes, and scientifically valuable mineral deposits.
  • Public Engagement & STEM Education: Demystifies NASA and ESA open planetary data by transforming raw PDS (Planetary Data System) archives into an engaging, visual "Google Earth for Mars" that inspires the next generation of explorers.

4. What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use?

  • Core Languages: TypeScript, JavaScript, Python 3.
  • Frontend Architecture: React 19, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Zustand (state orchestration), Lucide React icons.
  • Planetary GIS & Mapping Engine: @arcgis/core (ArcGIS Maps SDK for JavaScript) customised for non-terrestrial spheroids.
  • Data Engineering & ETL Pipelines: Python 3 using GDAL, Rasterio, GeoPandas, and Shapely for parsing PDS archives, processing DEM mosaics, and generating geodetic GeoJSON indexes.
  • Testing & Verification: Vitest, React Testing Library, and jsdom, backed by 334 automated tests (296 frontend unit/integration tests + 38 Python data pipeline tests).
  • Design System: Custom Obsidian Glass UI featuring high-contrast black glass panels, hairline specular borders, and zero-jitter tabular telemetry strips compliant with 100/100 Vercel Web Design Guidelines.

5. How is your project creative?

  • First-Person Ground "POV Cockpit": Moving beyond conventional top-down orbital views, ARES lets users drop down to ground level at any coordinate or rover waypoint, rendering realistic planetary scale, slope angles, and horizon contours from a rover’s vantage point.
  • Terrain-Aware Pathfinding Engine: Rather than drawing simple straight-line vectors, ARES integrates a geodetic lattice A* pathfinder that factors in terrain elevation changes (C=d⋅[1+wslope⋅(θ/θmax)2]C = d \cdot [1 + w_{\text{slope}} \cdot (\theta/\theta_{\text{max}})^2]C=d⋅[1+wslope​⋅(θ/θmax​)2]) to dynamically route vehicles around steep crater rims and escarpments.
  • Obsidian Glass Avionics HUD: Inspired by real aerospace cockpits and anti-slop design heuristics, the interface floats unobtrusively over the globe with responsive glass capsules, preserving maximum screen real estate for the planetary terrain.
  • In-Situ Scientific Dossiers: Every dataset is paired with an interactive provenance dossier linking direct PDS citations, operating sensor wavelengths, altimetry physics, and Martian chronostratigraphic epochs (Noachian, Hesperian, Amazonian).

6. What factors did your team consider?

  1. Geodetic Precision vs. Terrestrial Bias: Ensuring every formula uses the true Martian radius (a=3,396,190 ma = 3,396,190\text{ m}a=3,396,190 m, b=3,376,200 mb = 3,376,200\text{ m}b=3,376,200 m) so that distance and elevation calculations are mathematically exact.
  2. Scientific Honesty & Coverage Limits: High-resolution sensors like HiRISE cover only localised strips of Mars. When users zoom into areas lacking sub-metre coverage, ARES presents an explicit "Data unavailable for this extent" indicator rather than fabricating artificial textures.
  3. Network Performance & Progressive Streaming: Streaming multi-gigabyte planetary tiles over OGC WMTS/WMS endpoints requires robust retry mechanisms, tile fallback strategies, and responsive UI feedback to handle latency gracefully.
  4. Physical Rover Constraints: Factoring in realistic vehicle mobility limitations—such as maximum traversable slope thresholds (15°–25°), wheel traction risks on loose regolith, and rollover centre-of-gravity considerations.
  5. Human Interface Usability: Ensuring dark-adapted high contrast, mobile responsiveness (100dvh), keyboard accessibility (dismissals), and eliminating numerical jitter during map panning via tabular monospace typography.
